title: Toldot: room at last (Genesis 26:18–22)
hook: wells named Quarrel and Enmity, then Rehoboth, broad places

segments.voice: Yesterday, Toldot: two nations in one womb, the field and the tent. Your line was two in one womb. Today, Isaac digs.

The parking spot. The armrest on the plane. The neighbor's hedge, six inches over the line. Some fights are about real things. A lot of them are about who gets the space. Isaac, grown now, lives among the Philistines in a dry land, where water is everything. His father Abraham once dug wells there, and since then they've been stopped up with earth. So Isaac starts digging. And every time he finds water, somebody shows up to claim it.
screen: `WHO GETS THE SPACE?` → `WATER IN A DRY LAND.` → `ISAAC STARTS DIGGING.`

segments.voice: First, Isaac digs again the wells of his father, and here's a tender detail: he calls them by the same names his father had called them. Then his servants dig in the valley and find living water, a spring. The herdsmen of Gerar come and say: the water is ours. Isaac names that well Esek, contention. Quarrel. And he moves on. Another well, another fight. He names that one Sitnah, enmity, and moves on again. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't fight for either well. He gives each one an honest name, a record of what happened there, and he walks. Then they dig a third well, and this time, the text says, they didn't strive for it. He names it Rehoboth, from the Hebrew for broad, wide, open spaces. And he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land." Room, the gift at the end of all that digging. The medieval commentator Ramban read the three wells as a picture of Jewish history: two fought over, and a third, in the future, with room at last. Other readers keep it close to home. Some fights aren't worth winning. Moving on isn't the same as losing. And there's usually a Rehoboth somewhere, if you're willing to keep digging. Then the surprise: the king of the Philistines comes to Isaac and asks for a treaty. The man who walked away twice ends up with peace.
screen: `HIS FATHER'S WELLS, HIS FATHER'S NAMES.` · `ESEK: QUARREL. SITNAH: ENMITY.` · `REHOBOTH: BROAD PLACES.` · `THE KING COMES ASKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `THE LORD HATH MADE ROOM FOR US.`

segments.voice: Think of one running quarrel in your life: a group chat argument, a turf war at work, a family thing about who's right. Ask yourself honestly whether it's a well worth fighting for, or an Esek. If it's an Esek, picture yourself naming it and walking on, breathing into the open space on the other side.
Toldot. Generations: the portion where Isaac digs his father's wells, walks away from two fights, and finds Rehoboth, room at last.
Your line: there's room. Isaac found it at the third well he dug. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching prizes pursuing peace and avoiding needless quarrels, machloket, and Rehovot, a city in Israel, takes its name from Isaac's well of broad places.

chat.says: Isaac walked away from two wells people fought over. Isn't that just losing?
options: He named them Quarrel and Enmity and moved on; the third well brought room.
Yes. He was too weak to fight, so he gave up and went home.

chat.meaning: Isaac gave each fought-over well an honest name and walked on. At Rehoboth nobody strove: now the LORD has made room for us.
